text:
**Recommendation:** Spend the two engineer-weeks (10 person-days) in this order: measure and quarantine first, fix the highest-impact flaky tests second, cut CI time third, and adopt a standing rule in week six. The first move that restores trust is not fixing tests but making a red build mean something again, so quarantine comes before repair. Targets at week six: runs failing on non-deterministic causes fall from ~8% to under 1.5%; median CI time falls from 45 to under 20 minutes (p90 under 25); whole-pipeline re-runs fall by at least 80%; and every test left in the blocking suite has a measured pass rate above 99.5% over the previous 30 runs.

**Week 1: baseline (about 1.5 person-days).** You cannot fix what you have not counted, and the 8% figure is currently folklore. Pull the last 30 to 60 days of CI history (most CI systems expose this via API) and compute: (a) the share of pipeline runs that failed and then passed on re-run of the same commit, which is your true flake rate; (b) per-test failure counts, counting a test as flaky if it both failed and passed on the same commit; (c) per-stage and per-test duration, with the slowest 20 tests and the critical-path stage identified; (d) re-runs per merged PR and median time from first push to green. Then add lightweight instrumentation: have CI emit JUnit-style results to a shared store (a spreadsheet or small database is enough) so every run adds data, and record the failure message and runner ID alongside each result. Expect a skewed distribution: typically 10 to 25 tests cause most flakes, and browser tests are usually the worst offenders. The baseline also gives you the denominators for the week-six targets, so adjust them if the history shows something different, for example if 8% is already inflated by one infrastructure incident.

**Diagnosis before fixing (about 2 person-days, weeks 1-2).** First, use history: rank tests by flake count and by cost (flake count times the 45 minutes each re-run burns). Second, reproduce: run the top 25 candidates 50 to 100 times in isolation, then in the full suite in random order, then in parallel under CPU throttling. The pattern tells you the cause. Fails alone: timing or async waits. Passes alone but fails in the suite: shared state or order dependence. Fails only in parallel: shared resources such as ports, database rows or files. Fails only on CI runners: resource starvation or environment drift. Fails near midnight or month ends: clock dependence. Third, label every confirmed flake with one cause in the tracking sheet (timing, shared state, order, external dependency, environment, genuine product race). A genuine product race is the case worth watching for, because that flake is a real bug and deleting or retrying it hides it. Do not change any test during this phase except to add logging.

**Interventions, in order, with costs.** (1) Quarantine (1 day, week 2): move confirmed flaky tests into a non-blocking job that still runs and reports, each with an owner and a ticket. No deletion occurs, so the deletion constraint is respected; coverage is merely demoted temporarily. Immediately replace whole-pipeline re-runs with a re-run of failed jobs only, and cap automatic retries at one for browser tests while logging every retry, since retries that go unrecorded hide the very data you need. (2) Fix by cause, biggest offenders first (about 4 days across weeks 2-5): replace fixed sleeps with explicit waits on conditions; give each test its own data and clean up in teardown; stub the clock and network calls that leave the process; pin runner images and browser versions. Fix the top ten tests first, since they usually account for most flakes. Return each fixed test to the blocking suite only after 50 clean consecutive runs. (3) Retire only with cover (0.5 day): if a quarantined browser test duplicates behaviour already asserted at unit or integration level, delete it after you have named the covering test in the ticket; if the behaviour no longer exists, delete it and say so. Otherwise it stays and gets fixed or rewritten at a lower level.

**Bringing CI time down (about 2 days, weeks 3-5).** Use the week-one timing data rather than guessing. In rough order of payoff per day: run unit, integration and browser stages in parallel rather than in sequence, and shard browser tests across 3 or 4 runners (usually the single biggest saving); cache dependencies and build artefacts; run only fast unit and lint checks on every push and keep the full browser suite for merge to main and pre-merge on PRs touching relevant paths; replace slow UI-driven setup (logging in through the form, seeding through the interface) with API or database seeding; and push assertions down a level where a browser test is checking logic that a unit test could. Each of these preserves coverage. Target: under 20 minutes median. If parallelism raises runner cost, check that against budget before committing.

**Cost summary:** baseline 1.5 days, diagnosis 2, quarantine 1, fixes 4, covered deletions 0.5, CI time 2, rule and handover 0.5 to 1. That totals about 11.5 to 12, slightly over ten days, so the honest options are to fix fewer tests in weeks 4-5 (stop at the top 10 to 15) or to drop sharding until the flake rate is down. I recommend the former, since flake reduction is what restores trust. Spread the work as roughly 2 hours per engineer per week, with one person holding the tracking sheet.

**Rule that keeps it healthy (week 6 onward):** a test that fails and then passes on re-run of the same commit is a defect with a 7-day service level: it is quarantined automatically on its second such failure in 14 days, has a named owner, and returns to blocking only after 50 clean runs; any quarantined test older than 30 days is either fixed, replaced by named coverage and deleted, or deleted because the behaviour is gone. Add two guards: new tests must pass 20 consecutive runs before merging into the blocking suite, and the flake rate and median CI time are reviewed for ten minutes at each fortnightly retro, with a trigger that if the flake rate exceeds 3% for two weeks the team pauses features to fix it.

**Caveats and open questions:** the targets assume the flakes are concentrated; if the baseline shows them spread evenly across hundreds of tests, the cause is likely infrastructure (shared database, undersized runners) and the plan shifts toward fixing that environment instead. Product races may need real engineering beyond this budget; record them rather than quarantine silently. And if your CI vendor cannot export per-test history, budget an extra day for instrumentation.
